Time to normalization of gait following ACL reconstruction compared with
healthy controls: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Shiwei Chena,1
, Han Gongb,2
, Chennan Lyuc,3
, Kehan Lid,4
, Shazlin Shaharudina,*,5
a
School of Health Sciences, Universiti Sains Malaysia, Kelantan, Malaysia
b
School of Biological Science and Medical Engineering, Beihang University, Beijing Key Lab for Biomaterials and Neural Regeneration, Beijing, China
c
School of Physical Education, Wuhan Sports University, Wuhan, China
d
Department of Sports Studies, Universiti Putra Malaysia, Selangor, Malaysia
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Biomechanics
Longitudinal multilevel modeling
Knee functional recovery
Human health
Rehabilitation trajectory
A B S T R A C T
Background: Gait abnormalities often persist after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and may
increase the risk of reinjury and joint degeneration. This review aimed to assess differences in key gait param­
eters between ACLR patients and healthy controls, and to estimate when these parameters normalize
postoperatively.
Methods: Studies comparing individuals ≥3 months post–ACLR with healthy controls were included. A sys­
tematic search across five databases yielded 5251 records, with 20 studies (n= 976) retained. A longitudinal
multilevel meta-analysis was performed, with pooled effect sizes calculated using Cohen’s d, representing the
standardized mean difference. Postoperative time was modeled as a moderator in meta-regression analyses.
Results: Compared to healthy controls, ACLR patients assessed at 3–107 months postoperatively exhibited
significantly lower peak knee flexion angle (d = − 0.48, 95% CI: − 0.87 to − 0.10) and peak knee flexion moment
(d = − 1.06, 95 % CI: − 2.06 to − 0.07), while walking speed was non-significant (d = − 0.17, 95 % CI:
− 0.47–0.13). Logarithmic modeling indicated that group differences became non-significant at 16.2 months for
flexion angle and 10.1 months for flexion moment. Walking speed was statistically non-significant at any
timepoint.
Significance: At ≥ 3 months post-ACLR, patients exhibited significantly reduced peak knee flexion angle and
flexion moment compared to controls. These deficits normalized at approximately 16.2 and 10.1 months,
respectively. Walking speed did not significantly differ at any postoperative timepoint. These findings suggest
that early-phase rehabilitation should emphasize quadriceps strengthening and knee flexion restoration within
the first 10–16 months to address persistent biomechanical deficits.
1. Introduction
Injuries to the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) represent one of the
most frequent and serious forms of knee trauma in athletic populations
[1]. Epidemiological data indicate that tens of thousands of ACL rup­
tures occur annually, with an estimated incidence of 1 in 3500 per year
in the United States alone [2]. ACL injuries often lead to joint pain,
instability, and early-onset osteoarthritis, significantly impairing phys­
ical performance and quality of life [3].
Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is currently the
treatment of choice for restoring knee stability, with the primary
objective of enabling patients—particularly young athletes—to safely
return to sport [4]. Although most patients achieve clinical stability
following ACLR, gait recovery often remains incomplete in the short

term [5]. Research has demonstrated that ACLR patients commonly
exhibit biomechanical impairments during gait compared to healthy
controls [6], with persistent gait abnormalities frequently observed even
at 6–12 months postoperatively, and in some cases lasting up to two
years [7]. Such gait abnormalities not only increase the risk of ACL
re-injury but are also closely associated with postoperative joint
degeneration [7,8]. Therefore, identifying which gait parameters are
prone to long-term impairment and which parameters recover relatively
early following surgery is critical for evaluating rehabilitation progress
and developing targeted intervention strategies.
Currently, the findings regarding gait recovery following ACLR
remain inconsistent.For example, one study reported that ACLR patients
exhibited lower external knee flexion moment during walking compared
to healthy controls between 2 and 12 months postoperatively [9], while
another found that both knee flexion angle and joint moments were
higher in ACLR patients within the first 6 months post-surgery [10].
Although numerous studies have focused on alterations in joint loading
patterns during gait after ACLR, systematic summaries specifically
addressing the recovery timeline of gait parameters postoperatively
remain limited [11].
Therefore, a comprehensive synthesis of existing literature is neces­
sary to determine the critical time points at which key gait parameters
return to normal following ACLR, which is critical for optimizing
rehabilitation and guiding clinical assessment timing. Meta-analysis
provides a robust statistical framework to synthesize findings across
studies and to identify time-specific recovery trajectories following ACL
reconstruction [12], thereby making it well-suited to address this
question.
However, most existing meta-analyses have utilized traditional
frameworks, treating each study as an independent unit and extracting
effect sizes only at single time points [13], thus failing to fully leverage
data available from multiple follow-up assessments [14,15]. Conse­
quently, such approaches are insufficient to characterize the dynamic
trajectory of postoperative gait recovery.
To address these limitations, the present study aims to employ a
multilevel longitudinal meta-analytic approach. This method moves
beyond the traditional meta-analytic assumption of single effect-size
extraction by integrating data across multiple follow-up time points,
thus providing detailed insight into the temporal patterns of gait re­
covery. Given that current research on postoperative gait after ACLR
primarily focuses on core parameters such as walking speed, peak knee
flexion angle, and peak knee flexion moment [16–18], and considering
that consensus regarding their recovery trajectories has not yet been
reached [19], this study will specifically examine the dynamic changes
of these three parameters. Clarifying the time points at which these
parameters return to normal baseline value will provide robust evidence
to inform the optimization of postoperative rehabilitation strategies and
the establishment of clinical evaluation frameworks.
2. Methods
This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following
the PRISMA guidelines [20]. Additionally, the study protocol was
registered with the PROSPERO database (registration number:
CRD420251073937) on June 14, 2025.
2.1. Eligibility criteria
Participants included in this study were patients with primary ACL
rupture who underwent surgical reconstruction and had a postoperative
recovery period of at least three months. Each study needed to include a
healthy control group, ensuring baseline comparability between ACLR
patients and healthy individuals; comparisons must be made between
ACLR patients and healthy controls (i.e., between-subject comparisons).
Studies comparing reconstructed ACL limbs with the contralateral
healthy limbs (within-subject comparisons) were excluded to avoid bias
due to individual variability.
Studies had to report quantitative data for at least one of the
following gait-related parameters: peak knee flexion angle, peak knee
flexion moment, or walking speed. Additionally, studies needed to
explicitly identify the reconstructed limb.
2.2. Literature search and selection
After reviewing key literature to test appropriate terminology, our
search specifically targeted two elements: population (anterior cruciate
ligament reconstruction or ACL reconstruction or anterior cruciate lig­
ament or ACL) and outcomes ("gait" or "walking"). We systematically
searched PubMed, Embase, The Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and
EBSCOhost-SportDiscus using appropriate Medical Subject Headings
(Mesh) terms tailored to each database from database inception up to
February 28, 2025 (see Supplementary File 1). Additionally, relevant
meta-analyses on this topic were cross-referenced to identify further
original studies meeting our inclusion criteria.
2.3. Data extraction
Two independent pairs of reviewers (S.C. & H.G.; C. Lyu. & K.L.)
extracted data according to a customized data extraction table. Infor­
mation extracted included study design, basic demographic character­
istics (e.g., sample size, country, age, percentage of females, body mass
index, patient population), postoperative time points, and gait-related
outcome data (means and standard deviations for both experimental
and control groups). Since this was a longitudinal meta-analysis
comparing ACLR patients with healthy controls, all available time
points from long-term studies were extracted.
Upon completion of data extraction, the two reviewer pairs (S.C. &
H.G.; C. Lyu. & K.L.) performed cross-validation together with the cor­
responding author (S.S.). Any inconsistencies were resolved through
discussion within the research team, and relevant data were re-extracted
as necessary. Finally, the corresponding author (S.S.) conducted a
comprehensive review of all extracted data to ensure accuracy and
consistency.
2.4. Risk of bias and grade assessment
All studies included in this research were observational, comparing
gait parameters of ACLR patients with healthy controls (non- random­
ized controlled trials studies). Two pairs of reviewers (S.C. & H.G.; C.
Lyu. & K.L.) independently assessed the risk of bias using the Risk of Bias
In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool, evaluating
seven bias domains [21]. Any disagreements were resolved through
discussion with the corresponding author (S.S.).
To evaluate the overall certainty of evidence, we conducted a
structured evidence grading process using the GRADE (Grading of
Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) frame­
work, in accordance with the GRADE Working Group’s guidance for
non-randomized studies [22]. We systematically assessed five
domains—risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and
publication bias—for each outcome. Detailed outcome-specific GRADE
ratings are presentedin Supplementary File 2, indicating low to very low
certainty of evidence for peak knee flexion angle, peak knee flexion
moment, and walking speed.
2.5. Publication bias and sensitivity analysis
Funnel plot asymmetry and Egger’s regression test were used to
evaluate publication bias, with p>0.05 indicating no evidence of sig­
nificant bias [23]. Given that the longitudinal multilevel meta-analysis
incorporated multiple follow-up time points within individual studies,
we evaluated publication bias at two levels: first, within individual
studies (assessing data symmetry); second, across studies (evaluating
S. Chen et al. Gait & Posture 123 (2026) 109972
2

--- PAGE 3 ---
overall distribution symmetry) [24]. Sensitivity analyses were con­
ducted by systematically excluding each study to assess its individual
influence on the overall results, analyzing both within and between
studies.
2.6. Statistical analysis
To evaluate the temporal trends in gait parameters following ACL
reconstruction, we conducted a series of meta-analyses using RStudio.
First, pooled standard deviations (pooled SD) were calculated from the
means and standard deviations reported by experimental and control
groups. From these, standardized mean differences (SMD, Cohen’s d)
and their variances were computed to quantify effect sizes and statistical
uncertainty [25]. To account for correlation between multiple time
points within the same study, we assumed a correlation coefficient of
r=0.85, consistent with previous longitudinal meta-analyses in ACLR
patients [26]. This value was used to construct a within-study var­
iance-covariance matrix for the multilevel meta-analysis model. Cohen’s
d values were classified according to Cochrane Handbook thresholds:
<0.2 as trivial, 0.2–0.5 as small, >0.5–0.8 as moderate, and >0.8 as
large [27], facilitating comparisons between ACLR patients and healthy
controls at different time points.
A longitudinal mixed-effects meta-analysis was performed using the
restricted maximum likelihood (REML) method, primarily employing
the metafor package in R, following established analytical frameworks
[28,29]. To handle potential correlations across multiple follow-up time
points within different study cohorts, we developed multilevel
correlated-effect models [30]. The final model defined time points as
random effects nested within individual study cohorts and incorporated
a continuous autoregressive (CAR) structure to model temporal
correlations.
Subsequently, time points were included as fixed-effect moderators
to analyze trends in gait parameters over time. To identify the best
model fit, we explored various modeling strategies, including linear,
logarithmic-linear, 3-knot spline, and 4-knot spline models. Optimal
model selection was guided by criteria including Akaike Information
Criterion (AIC), Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), and visual in­
spection of fitted curves. Spline modeling was performed using the rms
package, with knot placement based on recommended guidelines [31].
Robust variance estimation for the final model was conducted using the
clubSandwich package [22].
The final results were presented as predicted effect sizes with their
95% confidence intervals, quantifying both magnitude and statistical
uncertainty. Additionally, the predict() function was used to estimate
effects at critical time points and to determine the time points at which
the effect sizes reached zero (i.e., statistical significance between ACLR
and control groups disappeared), thereby identifying critical milestones
for gait parameter recovery [32].
Detailed information about modelspecifications,parameters, scripts,
and all data is publicly available at: [https://github.com/Shiwei-Lab/
ACLR-Gait-Meta2025].
3. Results
3.1. Study selection and basic characteristics
As of February 28, 2025, a total of 5251 records were retrieved
through database searches. After initial screening, 70 potentially eligible
studies were identified. Following full-text review, 20 studies [11,14,15,
17,33–47,59] were ultimately included in the meta-analysis. A detailed
flowchart outlining the study selection process is presented in Fig. 1.
These 20 studies collectively involved 976 participants. All included
studies compared gait parameters between individuals with ACLR and
healthy controls, focusing primarily on peak knee flexion angle, peak
knee flexion moment, and walking speed. Postoperative follow-up pe­
riods for gait assessments ranged from 3 m to 107 months. Notably, 8
studies reported gait outcomes at multiple postoperative time points.
Key characteristics of the included studies are summarized in Table 2.
Fig. 1. PRISMA flow diagram of study selection. Flowchart outlining the literature screening process, including the number of records identified, screened, excluded
(with reasons), and the final studies included in the meta-analysis.

3.2. Risk of bias and publication bias
An overview of the risk of bias across included studies is provided in
Supplementary File 3. The majority of studies demonstrated methodo­
logical robustness in terms of intervention classification, handling of
missing data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting. However,
the quality of evidence was primarily affected by confounding factors
and selection bias. Specifically, only one study was rated as having a low
risk of bias [33]. Sixteen studies were judged to have a moderate risk of
bias, largely due to acceptable limitations in participant selection. Three

studies were assessed as high risk [41,45,59], primarily due to inade­
quate control of confounders and participant selection issues.
Regarding publication bias, funnel plots and Egger’s regression tests
are shown in Supplementary File 4. Under the conventional two-level
modeling framework, both peak knee flexion moment and walking
speed outcomes demonstrated marked asymmetry, with significant
Egger test results (p < 0.001), indicating left-skewed and right-skewed
distributions, respectively. In contrast, the distribution for peak knee
flexion angle appeared more symmetrical, with a non-significant Egger
test (p = 0.31), suggesting no substantial publication bias.
Under the multilevel meta-analytic framework, distributions for
peak knee flexion angle and peak knee flexion moment remained sym­
metrical, with non-significant Egger test results (p = 0.54 and p = 0.07,
respectively), indicating no notable publication bias. For walking speed,
however, Egger’s test yielded a significant result (p = 0.04), suggesting
potential but not definitive publication bias. Thus, evidence for publi­
cation bias in walking speed outcomes remains limited.
3.3. Main effects of gait parameters
3.3.1. Peak knee flexion angle
ACLR patients exhibited significantly lower peak knee flexion angles
during walking compared to controls (SMD = –0.48, 95 % CI: –0.87 to
–0.10*, p = 0.013). Heterogeneity analysis revealed substantial
between-study heterogeneity (τ² = 0.23, ρ = 0.90, Q = 25.55,
p = 0.004). Detailed results are presented in Supplementary File 5A
(forest plot and related model outputs).
3.3.2. Peak knee flexion moment
For peak knee flexion moment, ACLR patients showed significantly
lower values compared to healthy controls (SMD = –1.06, 95 % CI:
–2.06 to –0.07*, p = 0.04). Heterogeneity analysis again indicated
considerable between-study variability (τ² = 1.15, ρ = 0.88, Q = 29.20,
p < 0.001), as shown in Supplementary File 5B.
3.3.3. Walking speed
For walking speed, ACLR patients exhibited slightly reduced values
compared to controls, but the difference did not reach statistical sig­
nificance (SMD = –0.17, 95 % CI: –0.47–0.13, p = 0.28). Heterogeneity
was significant across studies (τ² = 0.14, ρ = 1.00, Q = 27.46, p = 0.01),
as shown in Supplementary File 5C.
3.4. Meta-regression results with postoperative time as a moderator
This analysis examined the relationship between postoperative time
and gait recovery by treating time as a moderator variable. The best-
fitting models were then used for final estimation.
3.4.1. Peak knee flexion angle
The effect of postoperative time on peak knee flexion angle was
assessed using a logarithmic model. Results indicated that time since
surgery was not a statistically significant moderator of peak knee flexion
angle (F = 1.99, p = 0.24). Although the trend suggested gradual
improvement in peak knee flexion angle over time, the regression co­
efficient did not reach statistical significance (k = 11, β = 0.21, 95 % CI:
–0.23–0.65, p = 0.24). As shown in Fig. 2(A).
3.4.2. Peak knee flexion moment
A logarithmic model was also employed to assess the influence of
postoperative time on peak knee flexion moment. The results similarly
showed no statistically significant moderating effect of time (F = 2.02,
p = 0.28). While the overall trend indicated some improvement in peak
knee flexion moment over time, the association was not statistically
significant (k = 7, β = 0.84, 95 % CI:–1.44–3.12, p = 0.28). As shown in
Fig. 2(B).
3.4.3. Walking speed
The relationship between postoperative time and walking speed was
evaluated using a linear model. The analysis revealed no statistically
significant trend (F = 0.14, p = 0.73). Although walking speed appeared
to improve slightly over time, the regression coefficient remained non-
significant (k = 13, β = 0.002, 95 % CI: –0.018–0.023, p = 0.73). As
shown in Fig. 2(C).
3.5. Trajectory of gait recovery at key postoperative time points
Gait recovery trajectories were further examined at five key post­
operative time points (3, 6, 12, 18, and 24 months) using model-based
predictions. Although spline and logarithmic models yielded similar
AIC/BIC values, the logarithmic model was ultimately selected for its
greater interpretability. The log function captures the nonlinear trend of
early rapid recovery followed by a plateau, which aligns with known
rehabilitation trajectories in ACLR patients. Additionally, it reduces the
risk of overfitting relative to spline models given the moderate number
of studies available at later time points.
3.5.1. Peak knee flexion angle
At 3 months postoperatively, ACLR patients exhibited significantly
lower peak knee flexion angles compared to healthy controls (SMD =
–0.75, 95 % CI: –1.33 to –0.18). This difference gradually diminished
over time: at 6 months (SMD = –0.61, 95 % CI: –1.04 to –0.18); 12
months (SMD = –0.46, 95 % CI: –0.84 to –0.08); 18 months (SMD =
–0.38, 95 % CI: –0.79–0.03); and 24 months (SMD = –0.32, 95 % CI:
–0.78–0.14). According to model-based predictions, the 95 % confi­
dence interval for the effect estimate first crossed zero at approximately
Fig. 2. Meta-regression of gait over time. Meta-regression plot showing the relationship between postoperative time and standardized mean differences (SMD) in gait
parameters. The curve represents the fitted longitudinal mixed-effects model with restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation. Shaded areas indicate 95 %
confidence intervals.

--- PAGE 6 ---
16.2 months, indicating that group differences in peak knee flexion
angle were no longer statistically significant beyond this time point.
Detailed results are provided in Table 1 and Fig. 3(A).
3.5.2. Peak knee flexion moment
At 3 months postoperatively, peak knee flexion moments in ACLR
patients were significantly lower than in healthy controls (SMD = –1.87,
95 % CI: –3.18 to –0.56). This difference lessened over time: at 6 months
(SMD = –1.29, 95 % CI: –2.17 to –0.42); 12 months (SMD = –0.71, 95 %
CI: –1.63–0.21); 18 months (SMD = –0.37, 95 % CI: –1.54–0.79); and 24
months (SMD = –0.13, 95 % CI: –1.52–1.26). According to the model’s
fitted predictions, the confidence interval for the effect estimate crossed
zero at approximately 10.1 months postoperatively, suggesting that
group differences in peak knee flexion moment were no longer statisti­
cally significant after this time point. Full results are shown in Table 1
and Fig. 3(B).
3.5.3. Walking speed
At 3 months postoperatively, ACLR patients demonstrated slightly
reduced walking speed relative to healthy controls (SMD = –0.28, 95 %
CI: –0.75–0.19). This trend of minimal difference persisted over time: at
6 months (SMD = –0.23, 95 % CI: –0.60–0.14); 12 months (SMD =
–0.19, 95 % CI: –0.50–0.13); 18 months (SMD = –0.16, 95 % CI:
–0.47–0.15); and 24 months (SMD = –0.14, 95 % CI: –0.46–0.18). At all
key time points, the 95 % confidence intervals crossed zero, indicating
that while walking speed showed a trend toward improvement over
time, none of the observed differences reached statistical significance.
Detailed data are presented in Table 1 and Fig. 3(C).
4. Discussion
4.1. Analysis of differences in gait parameters
4.1.1. Peak knee flexion angle differences
The results of this review indicate that ACLR patients exhibited
significantly reduced peak knee flexion angles during walking compared
to healthy controls, consistent with findings from existing systematic
reviews. Previous reviews reported generally lower peak knee flexion
angles in ACL-reconstructed patients compared to healthy individuals
during the postoperative period [53], and similar deficits have also been
reported during running at various stages of postoperative recovery [62,
63,65]. This limitation in flexion angles may be attributed to excessive
scarring and adhesions on the medial and lateral sides of the patella
following surgery [54]. Additionally, psychological factors such as pa­
tients’ fear of reinjury may reduce patients’ willingness or ability to fully
flex the knee [55]. Similarly, recent findings suggest that quadriceps
strength is associated with differences in knee flexion angle during gait
among individuals with ACLR [61], suggesting a possible link between
muscle function and knee flexion angle. Collectively, these factors likely
restrict the range of motion, thereby affecting knee flexion performance
during gait.
4.1.2. Peak knee flexion moment differences
Our review found that peak knee flexion moments were significantly
lower in ACLR patients compared to healthy controls, aligning with
trends reported in prior literature. Previous reviews highlighted that
reduced peak knee flexion moments commonly occur among ACL-
reconstructed patients for a period post-surgery [56]. This reduction
in peak knee flexion moment is potentially due to early postoperative
muscle atrophy, impaired neuromuscular control, and protective
compensatory strategies to avoid loading the reconstructed limb [57,
58]. These combined factors likely contribute to the observed deficit in
peak knee flexion moment during gait.
4.1.3. Walking speed differences
The present review noted that ACLR patients exhibited slightly lower
walking speeds compared to healthy controls, although the difference
was not statistically significant. This observation aligns with certain
previous studies, which reported no significant differences in spatio­
temporal gait parameters, including walking speed, between ACLR pa­
tients and healthy controls within 4–15 months post-surgery [59]. This
phenomenon might be explained by patients’ subjective adjustments
and compensatory mechanisms involving other joints [60], allowing
them to maintain nearly normal walking speeds despite incomplete knee
function recovery.
4.2. Recovery trends of gait parameters over time
4.2.1. Temporal changes in peak knee flexion angle
At 3 months postoperatively, ACLR patients showed significantly
lower knee flexion angles compared to healthy controls, indicating
noticeable asymmetry in sagittal plane movement between affected and
unaffected limbs in early postoperative gait [48]. Over time, these dif­
ferences gradually diminished and became statistically non-significant
at approximately 16.2 months, suggesting recovery of peak knee
flexion angle by the mid-term postoperative stage. This recovery trend is
consistent with previous research; for example, studies have shown that
both males and females exhibit abnormal peak knee flexion angles at 6
months post-ACLR, with normalization typically observed around 12
months [49]. However, some cross-sectional evidencesuggests that even
in the later stages of recovery—on average four years after surger­
y—ACLR patients may still exhibit reduced knee flexion angles during
running compared to healthy controls, indicating that full biomechan­
ical restoration may not occur in all individuals [64], with some studies
also reporting alterations in distal gait parameters such as foot pro­
gression angle and center of pressure trajectory during running [66].
The current findings further support the notion that peak knee flexion
angle recovery follows a dynamic trajectory characterized by early
Fig. 3. Trajectory of Gait Recovery at Key Postoperative Time Points. Predicted recovery trends for gait parameters across multiple postoperative timepoints. The
figure illustrates the point at which group differences become statistically non-significant, indicating functional normalization.
S. Chen et al. Gait & Posture 123 (2026) 109972
6

--- PAGE 7 ---
limitations followed by mid-term normalization, although long-term
deviations may persist in some cases.
4.2.2. Temporal changes in knee flexion moment
A similar temporal pattern was observed for peak knee flexion
moment. At 3 months postoperatively, ACLR patients exhibited signifi­
cantly reduced peak knee flexion moments compared to healthy con­
trols, reflecting early postoperativedeficits in neuromuscularoutput and
potential quadriceps avoidance behaviors [50]. The differences between
groups gradually decreased over time, becoming statistically
non-significant by approximately 10.1 months, suggesting mid-term
recovery. This trend aligns with previous studies, which have reported
an initial postoperative decline in peak knee joint moments followed by
gradual recovery toward normal levels [11]. Our review further re­
inforces the characterization of peak knee flexion moment recovery as
exhibiting early postoperative limitations followed by mid-term
recovery.
4.2.3. Temporal changes in walking speed
In contrast to the aforementioned parameters, walking speed did not
significantly differ between ACLR patients and healthy controls at any
critical postoperative time points, indicating a relatively rapid recovery
of walking speed postoperatively. This finding concurs with previous
research, which reported no significant differences in walking speeds
between ACLR patients and controls within 4–15 months post-surgery
[59]. It is noteworthy, however, that subtle gait adjustments, potentially
stemming from postoperative neuromuscular control changes [51], such
as asymmetries or alterations in specific gait phases [52], may still occur
despite the lack of overt differences in walking speed. Consequently,
when assessing the recovery of spatiotemporal gait parameters, atten­
tion should focus on gait symmetry and critical gait phases in ACLR
patients to more comprehensively reflect their functional recovery
status.
Although walking speed did not differ significantly between ACLR
patients and healthy controls in our analysis, this may not necessarily
indicate full walking speed recovery. Previous studies have suggested
that patients may adopt compensatory strategies—such as reducing
stride length or increasing cadence—to maintain a “normal” walking
speed despite persistent neuromuscular deficits and inter-limb asym­
metries [7,60]. These adjustments may mask underlying functional
limitations. Thus, walking speed alone may not be sensitive enough to
detect subtle gait asymmetries or functional limitations, and should be
interpreted in conjunction with other gait parameters.
4.3. Limitations and future directions
Given the limited and inconsistent reporting of acute postoperative
gait data, this study included only ACLR patients assessed at ≥ 3 months
post-surgery, potentially missing early-phase gait changes. Moreover,
uneven follow-up time distributions and small sample sizes at certain
intervals may have affected the precision of effect estimates.
Despite applying a multilevel modeling framework with continuous
autoregressive covariance and robust variance estimation to account for
within-study correlations, notable heterogeneity remained—particu­
larly for peak knee flexion moment (τ² = 1.15). This variability may
reflect differences in graft types, rehabilitation protocols, or follow-up
durations. However, insufficient reporting of these variables precluded
stratified analyses, limiting our ability to identify sources of heteroge­
neity. Additionally, the lack of standardized reporting for certain gait
parameters (e.g., phase-specific metrics) limited more comprehensive
exploration of motor control mechanisms.
Although including studies that used contralateral limbs as controls
may introduce additional sources of heterogeneity,it is also important to
acknowledge that excluding them and limiting the analysis to between-
group comparisons does not eliminate heterogeneity either.
Future research should focus on conducting high-quality,
prospective studies with extended follow-up periods, covering gait
changes across all postoperative phases following ACL reconstruction.
While the current study focused exclusively on gait-related parameters,
future work should aim to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of
knee function. Emphasis should be placed on detailed functional met­
rics, such as anterior-posterior (AP) joint stability, muscle strength, and
limb symmetry indices, to enable a more holistic assessment of func­
tional recovery.
5. Conclusion
This longitudinal multilevel meta-analysis synthesized evidence
across multiple postoperative time points to delineate the recovery
trajectories of key gait parameters following ACL reconstruction. At ≥ 3
months post-ACLR, patients demonstrated significantly reduced peak
knee flexion angle and peak knee flexion moment compared to healthy
controls. These deficits progressively resolved, reaching statistical
normalization at approximately 16.2 and 10.1 months, respectively.
Walking speed did not significantly differ at any postoperative time
point but may reflect compensatory strategies employed to maintain
normal gait. These findings highlight the importance of targeting
quadriceps strengthening and knee flexion restoration during early-
phase rehabilitation, particularly within the first 10–16 months, to
address persistent biomechanical deficits.
